`document questions` writes, from its title: the counts by
priority, the decisions each stakeholder must take and the material
each must provide, a material question counted only as the second,
the elements by origin when the specification tracks it,
the errors, one problem line each, when it has any, the decision
questions of what could be read grouped by stage in
life-cycle order and within a stage by priority then ID, then the
material questions in a group of their own, Material to provide, in
the same order (ADR-120), each with
who decides, or for material whom it is needed from, what it blocks (and for a blocked element, which keys
are missing there), the name it gives for the key it blocks with
the file and line of the element that leaves the key out, its
options, the decision that opened it when one did, with the
questions that decision answered, and so on back along the chain,
its Insight and Notes; then the references into other
specifications that are not resolved, each with where it stands,
the specification and version it names, and what it waits on (the
specification not given, or the must question that blocks the
element there); then, when
a source lists its clauses, the coverage: per such source, the
elements each clause produced, how many clauses produced nothing,
and the citations outside the listed clauses; then the outputs, one row per document target and per code target the
implementation files name, each ready, a draft (the questions and
the errors that concern it) or waiting (the errors, the questions,
and the approval that is missing or void), the questions given per
stage as how many and the first three by priority then ID.

**Insight:** The owner and the agent run validate after every edit, so validate counts the open questions and lists none; this verb is the list, with what each question holds up, so that the next decision is always in view. The same text is the document, because the people who decide read documents, not terminals.

**Note:** From ISO/IEC/IEEE 29148, Systems and software engineering, Life cycle processes, Requirements engineering, 2018, clause 6.6.3: The closure of to-be-determined and to-be-resolved items against plan is a measure of the requirements work. <https://www.iso.org/standard/72089.html>

```
specarch gaps <paths>...
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<paths>` | Folders holding specifications, searched as validate searches them. One or more. | yes |

It reads:

- `{paths}`: The specifications and their implementation files.
- `records/approvals/<version>.yaml`: The approval of the specification's version, beside its folder, when there is one.

It writes no file.

On standard output: The problems of each estate given, then the open questions document of each specification, with its errors listed in it.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, and the reason on an unreadable path.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | no must or should question is open and no specification has an error |   |
| 1 | at least one must or should question is open, or a specification or an estate has an error | Answer the open must and should questions it lists with specarch decide and settle the errors, then run it again. |
| 2 | usage error, or a path that could not be read | Read the usage message or the reason on standard error, correct the command line or the path it names, and run it again. |

### specarch generate

Write code or data from a specification.

Validates its input first and writes nothing from an invalid
specification. Without `--out`, passes over a specification whose
implementation files name no output folder for the target, with a
warning of rule output_folder at their targets, as document does
(ADR-073), and exits 2 when every specification given is passed
over. Then refuses, with status 1, while a must or should question
blocks a section the target reads: the sections the implementation
file names under `targets.<target>.reads`, or every section when it
names none. Then refuses, with status 1, when
`records/approvals/<version>.yaml` is missing or its digest is not the
digest of the specification's files now. `--unapproved` lets the run
through both refusals and makes the output a draft: every file says
it is one, naming the questions that block what the target reads and
the approval's state, and a draft exits 0 (ADR-066, ADR-086). Then
writes the target into the folder it owns, and nothing outside it.
With `--check` nothing is written: the output is made in memory and
compared with what is on disk. A generated file, one whose text has
the line that starts the generated header, is compared byte for
byte. A file with no such line was built by hand: it matches when it
equals what the target writes without the header, the draft notice
and the problem marks, and a match is named in a line of its own and
not counted as differing. A file the plug-in marks as an object
literal is, when it differs, read on both sides in the subset of
TypeScript that is also JSON5 (ADR-093) and compared by value: the
imports, the exported constant's name, the type it satisfies and the
literal. A hand-built one with equal values matches; for any other,
each differing value is printed below the file's line, by its path
in the literal, with the value on disk and the one generated; any
other file built by hand that differs names its first differing
line, both ways. A file
on disk outside the subset is not comparable, named with its line
and what was found there, and counts as differing.

A target this program does not build in is produced by a plug-in found
on PATH. For each implementation file that names the target under
`targets` (every implementation file when none does), the plug-in is
`specarch-gen-<target>-<stack>` when there is one, where the stack is
first the target's `framework` in lower case, given under
`targets.<target>.framework` or the platform's default when the
target names a platform and no framework (plain-javascript on web,
swiftui on iphone), then the file's `stack.language.name` in lower
case with a dash for a space, and `specarch-gen-<target>` otherwise;
none found is status 2. A framework is a stack of the file, as a
dialect is, so one language may have a plug-in per framework. Files
that find the same plug-in and name the same output folder run it
together, a file that names none joining the others of its plug-in,
and each run writes into the folder its files name, so `--out` is
refused when the files reach more than one plug-in or folder. The program runs each plug-in once per
specification with a request on its standard input, as JSON:
`specarch` (the meta-model version), `target`, `root` (the root file's
path), `specification` (the merged, validated specification as plain
values), `implementations` (each implementation file as `file`,
`content`, the target's `settings` from it, and `idioms`, the idioms
it uses, each with its `name`, `version`, how it applies (`as`:
shipped, overridden, project or excluded), the `content` of the idiom
that applies and the project's `override`) and `output` (the folder
the files are for), and `existing`, the text files already in that
folder by their path in it, so a plug-in that adds files, such as a
migration beside a snapshot, knows what is there without reading the
disk; `draft`, the notice every file of a draft carries, from
"Draft:" to "this file is not the approved output", or empty for the
approved output; and `problems`, the specification's warnings and
open questions in the order of its problems file, each with its
`id`, `severity`, `rule`, `message`, the `pointer` into the merged
specification it is marked at (empty for a problem outside it, such
as in an implementation file) and, for a question, what it
`blocks`, so the output marks each one at the entry it shows for it
(docs/diagnostics.md); and `check`, true when the run only compares,
so a plug-in that refuses to write over a file built by hand answers
its files for the comparison. The plug-in answers on its standard output,
as JSON, with `files` (each a `path` relative to the output folder,
its `content`, and `comparison: object-literal` for a file that is
one object literal of data, which `--check` compares by value) and `diagnostics` (each with the validator's fields:
file, line, severity, path, rule, message, and a column when it
knows one), and exits 0. The program places each diagnostic at its
entry: one at the root file, whose path leads to an entry of the
merged specification, is put at the fragment, line and column that
entry was read from; a column not given is derived as validate
derives it; and the id is made as validate makes it. It prints the
diagnostics in validate's line, refuses a path outside the output folder,
and writes or checks the files itself. When the plug-in answers
with diagnostics, the program runs it once more with them added to
`problems`, each with its id and `target: true`, so the files mark
the target's own problems as well; it writes what that run answers.
A plug-in that cannot express an entry answers the rest of its
output with that entry marked, and an error makes the run exit 1
after the files are written or checked; a plug-in that can write
nothing answers no file (ADR-086). A plug-in that exits with
another status, or answers with something else, fails the run with
status 2; its standard error is passed through.

An element whose mapping in the implementation file names a
stakeholder under `ownedBy` is owned by that stakeholder: a plug-in
that builds code or data writes nothing for it or for anything under
its pointer, and an element that refers to it still refers to it; the
tests target, which checks rather than builds, keeps it (ADR-046). The gate does not look
at the mark, so a question that blocks an owned element still holds
the target up.

**Insight:** One program with verbs, and generators as plug-ins found on PATH, is the pattern of protoc, git and kubectl: one name to learn and install, one parser, one diagnostic format and one version shared by every target, and new targets added without changing the program. Letting the program write the files, as protoc does, keeps `--check` and the rule "only into its folder" true for every plug-in without each one having to implement them.

**Note:** From Protocol buffers compiler plug-in protocol, plugin.proto, 2024: A plug-in reads a CodeGeneratorRequest from standard input and writes a CodeGeneratorResponse to standard output; the file names it answers are relative to the output directory, and protoc writes them. <https://github.com/protocolbuffers/protobuf/blob/main/src/google/protobuf/compiler/plugin.proto>

```
specarch generate <target> <paths>... [--out <out>] [--check] [--unapproved]
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<target>` | A code or data target, built in or offered by a plug-in; kebab-case. | yes |
| `<paths>` | Folders holding specifications, searched as validate searches them. One or more. | yes |

| Option | What it does | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--out <out>` | The folder the target owns. Without it, the folder the implementation files' `targets` name for the target, relative to each implementation file; they must agree. |  |
| `--check` | Make the output in memory and fail when the files on disk differ. Writes nothing. |  |
| `--unapproved` | Write a draft from a specification that is not approved yet, because no approval record covers its files as they are or an open must or should question blocks what the target reads. The refusal is the default; with this, every file says it is a draft and why. |  |

It reads:

- `{paths}`: The specifications and their implementation files.
- `records/approvals/<version>.yaml`: The approval of the specification's version, beside its folder.
- `{out}`: The current output, with `--check`.
- `specarch-gen-{target} on PATH`: The plug-in for a target that is not built in.

It writes:

- `{out}/`: The files the target produces, as the plug-in answers them. Nothing is written with `--check`.

On standard output: The diagnostics of an invalid specification, the output_folder
warning of each specification passed over, and the diagnostics the
plug-in answers with, one line each. With `--check`, one line per
file that differs, is missing or is not comparable, each differing
value of an object literal on an indented line below it, and for
any other file built by hand its first differing line, and one line
per file built by hand that matches.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, the reason a plug-in was not found or failed (its path and exit status, or the start of an answer that is not JSON), each file the plug-in is not given because it cannot be read and why, one line per step when a run takes more than one plug-in or output folder (N of M), the plug-in's own standard error, and a one-line count at the end.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | written, a draft included, or with `--check` the output is current |   |
| 1 | a specification has an error, an open question blocks what the target reads or the specification is not approved and `--unapproved` was not given, the plug-in reported an error (what it answered is written or checked), or with `--check` the output differs | Settle the errors, answer the questions that block the target, or approve the specification with specarch approve; with --check, run it once without --check to write the current output. |
| 2 | usage error, no generator for the target (not built in and no plug-in on PATH), the plug-in failed or answered badly, no output folder in any specification given, or a file that could not be read or written | Put the plug-in specarch-gen-<target> on PATH, name an output folder for the target in an implementation file, or correct the command line, and run it again. |

### specarch idioms

List the idioms each implementation file uses, and how.

Validates its input first and prints nothing but the errors from a
specification that has them. Then prints, for every implementation
file of every specification, its path and one line per idiom: every
shipped idiom and every one of the project's own that applies to the
file, by its stacks and by the keywords the specification uses, with
its version and how it applies: shipped, overridden (by which file,
copied from which version, replacing which parts), the project's own,
or excluded; an override's or an exclusion's reason follows.

**Insight:** The shipped idioms apply without a word in the implementation file, so a reader needs one place that says which ones do, and where the project deviates.

```
specarch idioms <paths>...
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<paths>` | Folders holding specifications, searched as validate searches them. One or more. | yes |

It reads:

- `{paths}`: The specifications, their implementation files, and the idioms folder beside each.

It writes no file.

On standard output: The errors of an invalid specification, one line each; otherwise each implementation file's path and its idioms, one per line.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, and the reason on an unreadable path.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | the idioms were listed |   |
| 2 | usage error, a path that could not be read, or a specification with errors | Run specarch validate and settle its errors, or correct the path it names, then run it again. |

### specarch idioms diff

Print a shipped idiom's parts beside each override's.

Validates its input first, as idioms does. Then, for every
implementation file that overrides the named idiom, prints the
override's file, the version it was copied from and the version this
program ships, and for each part it replaces and each stack the
override renders, the shipped rendering and then the override's, as
YAML. With no override of the idiom, it says so.

**Insight:** An override records the version it was copied from, and the validator warns when a newer one ships; this is how the project sees what changed before it moves.

```
specarch idioms diff <idiom> <paths>...
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<idiom>` | The name of a shipped idiom. | yes |
| `<paths>` | Folders holding specifications, searched as validate searches them. One or more. | yes |

It reads:

- `{paths}`: The specifications, their implementation files, and the idioms folder beside each.

It writes no file.

On standard output: The errors of an invalid specification, one line each; otherwise each override with the shipped and the overriding renderings of what it replaces.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, the reason on an unreadable path, and that the idiom is not shipped.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | the overrides were printed, or there was none |   |
| 2 | usage error, an idiom this program does not ship, a path that could not be read, or a specification with errors | Run specarch validate and settle its errors, or correct the idiom's name or the path it names, then run it again. |

### specarch merge

Merge the partial specifications the readers wrote into one.

Reads two or more partial specification trees, each written by
`specarch extract` or by hand from documents, and writes one
specification that holds every element of them, following
`docs/from-sources.md`, section 3.2. Each tree is checked on its own
first: a tree that does not track origin, that validate reports an
error in, that holds implementation files or records, or that holds
a test other than the drafts specarch derive writes for that tree is
refused. A test is one of those drafts when its name and values are
those of the draft derive writes for the tree without its tests; the
problem marks above its entries do not count. The drafts are left
out, since they are derived from one tree alone, and the derivation
runs again into the merged specification, as extract runs it
(ADR-055).

- The same element in two trees (an entry of a section by its name,
  an operation by its path and method, a field by its entity and
  name) becomes one element with the citations of both. A key only
  one tree writes is kept. A key the trees give different values is
  left out, and a must question cites both and blocks it. A
  field's `type` is kept instead, since a field is not read without
  one (ADR-122): the union of the types where they differ only in
  whether null is allowed, else the first tree's type, with the
  other trees' keys that go with their types (a format, a width, a
  pattern, the values, a default or an example, the items, the
  properties) left out with them; the question says what was kept and names each key left
  out, and a line names the type kept. A role's `permissions` are
  joined grant by grant once every tree is in, on the permissions
  the trees declare (ADR-127): a tree's list says nothing of a
  permission the tree does not declare, so the merged list is the
  first tree's, then what each later tree adds, with every tree's
  citation, and a line names the trees whose grants add up. A
  permission one tree grants that another tree, which has the
  role, declares and does not grant is a disagreement: the list is
  left out, and the must question names each such permission with
  the trees that grant it and the trees that withhold it, and
  blocks, as well, each permission the lists name that no merged
  role grants, itself or through a permission it implies. A role a
  printed and a parsed tree both give is compared below instead.
  The merged specification always passes validate. An
  entity's `required` is compared field by field: a field only one
  tree has keeps what that tree says, and a field both have that
  one requires and the other does not is left out of `required`,
  with a must question on that field that blocks the entity's
  `required`.
- A position where one tree refers to a named schema, entity or
  enum and another writes the shape in place is settled once every
  tree is in (ADR-117). The named shape and the one written in place
  are compared on what both say: the keys that say what a value is,
  `required` and `enum` as sets, the items, and each property both
  list, through a property that is a reference on one side. Where
  nothing both say differs, the reference is kept and a line names
  the trees that refer and the trees that write; where a key both
  give differs, the key is left out and the must question above
  names each difference; where only the properties listed differ,
  the reference is kept and a should question at the position names
  the properties each side lists and the other does not. A tree's
  question at that position is answered by the trees that refer;
  one below it follows the reference to the named entry, or moves
  up to the position where the key is left out. An entity's field
  left out so leaves the entity's `required` list too.
- A name one tree gives to a schema and another to an entity or a
  view, or one to a view and another to an entity, is kept in both
  entries, each as its trees give it, since a schema, an entity and
  a view are one namespace and the merge does not know whether the
  shape is the record (ADR-132). One must question per such schema
  or view asks whether the name is one element or two, with an
  option that makes it the entity or the view it is named like,
  where what refers to the one refers to the other, and an option
  that gives it another name; its why names the trees that give the
  name each way, it cites both entries, and it blocks the schema or
  the view, where the validator reports the error it holds while
  the question is open. A line names the question.
- An entity's field holding a schema in columns is written out as
  `specarch generate sql` writes it, every part's column and the
  check that an optional value is wholly absent or has its required
  parts, and compared with the code side's fields (ADR-077). Where
  every part's column is there with the type, width and nullability
  its part gives it, every check of the entity naming one of them is
  such a presence check, and every presence check the field writes
  is there, the columns, their place in `required` and those checks
  are left out, the field is the code's too, and a line names them;
  a key only the column gives is written into the part, and a part
  that refers to an enum or a schema is compared on its nullability
  only. A tree's question on a column or a check read back so, or on
  a JSON column read as a schema, is left out with a line. Where only
  some parts have a column, a column differs from its part, another
  check names one, a presence check is missing, or the field is held
  as json and has columns, nothing is joined and a must
  question at the field names each difference. A field one tree
  gives as a schema and another as an object is that schema with
  storage json. Where no tree has a field holding a schema, and an
  entity's code-side fields are every part's column of a schema
  under one prefix, a should question at those fields asks whether
  they are one value, a field named after the prefix, or fields of
  their own.
- An element is stated when a tree states it; it is inferred only
  when every tree that has it infers it.
- A tree whose sources are all code is on the code side; any other
  tree is on the documents side. Where both sides are merged, an
  element of a design section that only one side has is compared
  with the other side when that side has elements in the same
  section, or, for a field, the same entity. Only the code has it:
  it is written inferred, with a why that starts "Undocumented, from
  code." and names where, and a question asks the owner to confirm
  it; a field, which holds no origin of its own, is written as the
  code has it, and only the question says so. Only the documents have it: it is written as they state it,
  and a question in `implementation/questions.yaml`, blocking
  `implementation`, starts "Not built yet." and cites the documents
  and the code that was read. Either question is must when the
  element concerns security (a role, a permission, an operation, or
  an entity or field that is personal or a credential) or when a
  source it cites is marked `givenOutside`; otherwise it is should.
- A requirement of the documents side whose statement gives one
  number of days, such as "The loan period is 21 days.", is compared
  with the check constraints of the code side that move a date by
  exactly one number of whole days. When exactly one such check has
  every word of the statement's subject in its name (the words
  before is, are, shall, must, will or should, without the, a, an,
  of, each and every), the check satisfies the requirement. The
  words, the number words and the units of whole days, such as
  days and weeks, are the vocabulary's of the language of the
  source the requirement cites first (`docs/vocabularies.md`):
  English when the source names none, the one SpecArch ships for
  it, or the one given with `--vocabulary`; a language with none is
  said once and its requirements are not compared. When the
  numbers differ, the requirement's statement is left out and one
  must question cites both and blocks it; the check keeps the
  expression the code runs. No match, or more than one, changes
  nothing (ADR-048).
- A code source says how it was read: `reading: printed` for a list
  the running system printed, such as a route table or the document
  dxlib emits, `reading: parsed` for source read by a parser
  (ADR-075). A tree whose code sources all say the same reading
  has it. Where a printed and a parsed tree both have operations,
  an operation only the parsed tree declares keeps what it states,
  and a must question that starts "Declared, not
  registered:" cites the line that declares it and names the
  printed trees, since the running system does not list it: the
  code is never reached, or only under a setting, or the printer
  misses it. An operation only the printed trees have keeps its
  citations, and a could question that starts "Registered by code
  the reader does not follow:" cites them. Entities and roles are
  compared the same way where a printed and a parsed tree both have
  them: an entity only the source declares is a must question that
  starts "Declared, not in the database:", one only the catalogue
  holds a could question that starts "In the database, declared
  nowhere the reader follows:"; a role only a seed grants is a must
  question that starts "Seeded, not granted:", one only the
  permission table holds a could question that starts "Granted,
  seeded nowhere the reader follows:". A role both give grants what
  the printed trees grant, since that is what the check reads, with
  every tree's citation and no disagreement asked on its list; a
  grant only a seed makes is a must question that starts "Seeded,
  not granted:" blocking the role's permissions and the permission,
  and one only the table holds a could question that starts
  "Granted, seeded nowhere the reader follows:".
- A tree whose roles grant permissions says how its roles go on the
  wire: with info.roleNames when its reader found them in upper
  snake case, and without it when it found them as named. Where two
  such trees say different things, the merge leaves info.roleNames
  out and asks one must question blocking roles, naming each way
  and the trees that say it (ADR-112). A tree with no role that
  grants a permission says nothing of it. info.wireNames is taken
  from the tree that names it, as before: a tree whose reader saw
  no wire leaves it out without saying the names go as written.
- Every reader asks about a check that lets every request through
  while a setting is empty in the same words, "The check <check>
  runs only when the setting <setting> is present." (or "is true."
  for a boolean setting). Where a printed
  and a parsed tree both ask about one check, by its name, the merge
  asks it once with every tree's citation, and names both settings
  when they differ. One only the parsed tree asks, where a printed
  tree holds roles, is a must question that adds that the
  permission table does not declare the gate; one only the printed
  tree asks, where a parsed tree holds operations, keeps its
  question and adds a could question that starts "Declared, not
  found:", since the check's code is outside the middlewares the
  parser reads.
- Every reader asks about a check skipped for one kind of caller in
  the same words, "The check <check> is skipped for every
  <kind>:" (ADR-114). The merge asks it once per check and kind,
  blocking the permission of every operation any tree says the
  check guards, with every tree's citation, and never leaves it out
  as answered: a tree that gives an operation's permission does not
  say whether that kind of caller is meant to reach it.
- A parsed tree's must question that blocks one of its own
  operations, entities or roles and nothing else asks whether the
  running system registers it, holds it or grants it. A printed
  tree that gives the element answers it, and it is left out with a
  line naming that tree; where printed trees have elements of that
  section and not this one, it is left out too, and the question of
  the row above asks it with what they printed.
- Sources of the same key are one source when they are the same in
  everything but their clauses, which are joined, and their
  reading: the merged source keeps a reading every tree gives it
  and says none when one tree read it printed and another parsed. Code sources that
  differ only in their edition are one repository read at different
  commits: the merged edition is the newest of them, which each
  other is an ancestor of, and every path a tree read must be
  unchanged from the commit it was read at up to it. Sources of the
  same key that differ otherwise are refused.
- Where both sides have operations, a documents-side source none of
  whose operations' paths the code side has, such as an OpenAPI file
  left from a template, is reported as a placeholder, with the
  number of its paths; its operations are compared as any other
  (ADR-049).
- A question of a tree whose every blocked key another tree gives
  is left out, since that tree answers it and the element cites
  both; a question that blocks a stage, an element or a key no tree
  gives is kept (ADR-049). An element the asking tree writes only by
  name, as an empty mapping, is one it does not give, so a tree that
  gives it with content answers the question, such as a field a page
  shows whose type the database gives (ADR-057).
- A question whose every block is the section `gateways`, the
  question a code reader asks at a fallback handler or a catch-all
  route, is left out as answered when another tree declares a
  gateway for it, as the tree `specarch extract gateway` writes
  from a gateway table does: that tree says what the handler
  forwards and by which claim, and the line names the trees and the
  gateway (ADR-142, ADR-143). Each gateway answers one such question
  over the whole merge, never one of its own tree, since one gateway
  table describes one gateway in front of one tree: first the
  questions at a fallback handler in every tree, then those at a
  catch-all route, which may as well be a file server, in every
  tree, each pass over the trees in the order given and in each
  tree in the order it asks them, so a catch-all question never
  takes a gateway from another tree's fallback question. A question no gateway is left for stays
  open, with a line that says so, rather than being answered by a
  gateway that has nothing to do with it.
- A map one tree writes open, `additionalProperties: true`, with a
  question of that tree blocking that key, and another tree writes
  with a value type, takes the value type with no disagreement, in
  whichever order the trees are given: the open map is unknown, not
  a claim. The asking tree's question is left out as answered, with
  a line naming the trees that give the type. A tree that writes
  the map open and asks nothing says its values may be anything,
  and two value types are two claims: either is a disagreement, as
  `false` against `true` or a type is (ADR-126).
- A question of a tree that names, under `names`, the operation a
  key it blocks refers to, such as a workflow's trigger or a step's
  operation, or a page's source or submit, is left out as joined
  when another tree declares an operation of that name: the name is
  written at the key, where the design schema puts it, and the line
  names the trees that declare it. A name no tree declares keeps
  its question.
- A question of a tree whose every blocked key a question kept
  before it blocks, with the same priority, is left out, since both
  ask the same thing, such as a permission's description that the
  router and the permissions reader each ask for (ADR-050). A
  could question is never left out so: it holds nothing, and two
  at one entry are two things a reader could not hold there.
- Where the code side has operations, a permission a role grants
  and no operation, command or page checks is reported with the
  roles that grant it, since a grant nothing checks is either left
  from code that was removed or guards something the routes do not
  show (ADR-050).
- The questions of the trees are numbered again, Q-1 upward, in the
  order the trees are given, and the merge's own questions follow.
  Every element keeps the file its first tree wrote it in.
- The same trees in the same order give byte-identical output.

**Insight:** The readers write one tree per surface so that each is checked on its own; the comparison between surfaces, and between the documents and the code, is made once, here, where a disagreement becomes a question rather than a choice.

```
specarch merge <trees>... --out <out> [--vocabulary <vocabulary>]
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<trees>` | The partial specification trees to merge, each a folder holding specarch.yaml, in the order their questions are numbered. One or more. | yes |

| Option | What it does | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `--out <out>` | The folder the merged specification is written into; it becomes the specification's root folder. | yes |
| `--vocabulary <vocabulary>` | A vocabulary file (docs/vocabularies.md) for a language SpecArch ships none for, by which the requirements of the sources in that language are compared with the code's checks; repeated, one per language. |  |

It reads:

- `{trees}`: The partial specification trees.

It writes:

- `{out}/`: The merged specification, each problem validate finds in it and each open question marked above its entry with a `# specarch-problem:` line, as document problems marks a fragment (ADR-066); the marks of the trees read are not carried over.

On standard output: One line per tree naming its title, its side, its reading where it
has one, and what it holds; one line per
source joined from several trees, naming the edition taken; one line
per role whose grants several trees add up, naming the trees; one line
counting the elements written and those found in more than one
tree; one line per position where a reference and a shape written
in place meet, saying whether the reference is kept or the key left
out; one line per source whose language has no vocabulary, saying
its requirements' days are not compared; one line per field read back from its columns, and one per
question that what was read back answers; one line per requirement joined to a check that gives the
same number of days; one line per question of a tree that another
tree answers or a question kept before it asks, and per parsed
tree's question on whether the running system registers an
operation, holds a table or grants a role that a printed tree
answers or the merge asks again; one line per gate question joined
or asked again, and per question on a bypassed check joined; one
line per
question whose name is joined to the operation another tree
declares; one line per
placeholder source; one line per permission granted and checked by
nothing; one line per
question the merge asked, naming what it blocks and why; and the
lines of the derivation, as extract prints them.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, and the reason a tree could not be merged.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | the merged specification was written |   |
| 1 | a tree could not be merged: it does not track origin, validate reports an error in it, it holds implementation files or records or a test that is not the draft derive writes for it, or it declares a source another tree declares differently, or whose paths changed after the commit a tree read them at; or a vocabulary that is not one this build reads | Read the reason on standard error and settle the tree it names, running specarch validate on it, then run it again. |
| 2 | usage error, fewer than two trees, two vocabularies of one language, or a folder or file that could not be read or written | Read the usage message or the reason on standard error, correct the command line or the path it names, and run it again. |

### specarch model

Print the specifications as one JSON document, for a program.

Reads the specifications, implementation files and estates found
under the paths given, as validate finds them, and prints one JSON
document in RFC 8785's canonical form: object members sorted by
their names as UTF-16 code units, no whitespace, every number as
ECMAScript prints a double, then a newline. It is how an editor or
another program reads a specification as specarch reads it, without
a loader of its own, and both builds print the same bytes.

The document holds `specarchModel`, the version of its shape, `0.1`;
`program`, the program version; `specifications`, one per root file,
sorted by it; `implementations`, the implementation files outside
any specification; and `estates`, each estate file with its modules.

A specification has its `root` file, its `name` and `version` from
`info` and its `metaModel` from `specarch`, each null when the file
gives none; the merged `document` as plain values, what the schema
validates; `positions`, which maps the JSON pointer of every node,
`/` for the whole document as the problems file writes it, to the
`file`, `line` and `column` where it starts: its key in a mapping, or
the item in a list; `references`, every reference that resolves to an
element of the specification, in document order, each with `from`,
the pointer of the entry that refers, `to`, the pointer of the element,
and `through`, the keyword that made it; `problems`, the problems
found while reading it, such as a folder that is not a stage, a
section in the wrong stage or a file that does not parse, in the
problems file's form (`file`, `line`, `column`, `severity`, `path`,
`rule`, `message`, `id`); and `implementations`, each implementation
file inside it.

The references are made by `$ref`, when it is a pointer into the
specification; by `satisfies`, `verifies` and `decidedIn` wherever
they stand; and by the keywords that name an element by its name
where the meta-model puts them: a relation's `target`, a guard's or a
list's `entity`, a page's `entity`, a job's or a command's `reads` and
`writes`, a workflow's `subject` and a test's `entity` name an entity
or a view; `permission` on an operation, a command, a page, a page's
action and a workflow's step, and a role's `permissions`, name a
permission; a job's `role`, an approval's `approvers`, a client's
`roles` and a signer's `role` name a role; `emits` on an operation, a
job and a workflow, and a job trigger's `consumes`, name a channel's
message; `calls` names a dependency; a menu's or a flow step's `page`
and a test's `page` name a page; a workflow's `trigger`, a workflow
step's `operation` and a test's `operation` name an operation by its
operationId; and `callers`, `token`, `handshake`, `middlewares`, and a
test's `command`, `job`, `workflow`, `flow` and `requirement` name the
element of their section. A reference that does not resolve is a
problem of validate and is not listed; nor is a reference into
another specification.

An implementation file has its `file`, its `stack`, its `document`,
its `positions`, its `references`, the design pointers under
`implements` and a mapping's `design` that resolve in the
specification it is in, and its `problems`, what of its YAML does
not parse. An estate's module has its `name`, its `location` and
`version` as the estate writes them, and `specification`, the root
file of the specification read for it, or null.

The validator's errors and warnings are not in the document: the
problems file and its SARIF form are their one list. A specification
that does not validate is printed all the same, with every problem
found while reading it.

**Insight:** An editor shows a specification as specarch reads it only when it reads it through specarch; a second loader in another language would drift from the first.

```
specarch model <paths>...
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<paths>` | Folders and files, as validate takes them. One or more. | yes |

It reads:

- `{paths}`: Root files, the files under their stage folders, implementation files and estates.
- `each estate's modules, at their location`: The specification of every module an estate lists, read with the estate.

It writes no file.

On standard output: One JSON document in RFC 8785's canonical form, then a newline.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, and the reason on a path that could not be read.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | printed |   |
| 2 | usage error, a path could not be read, or a folder holds no specification, no implementation file and no estate | Read the usage message or the reason on standard error, correct the command line or the path it names, and run it again. |

### specarch validate

Check specifications and implementation files.

Checks every specification found under the paths given: a folder that
holds `specarch.yaml` is one specification, read as a whole, including
the implementation files under its `implementation/` folder; nothing
under it is searched further, so a test folder's data files are never
read as specifications. An implementation file outside any
specification is checked on its own against the specification its
`implements` names. A file given by name must be a root file or an
implementation file; a fragment of a tree is refused with the folder
to run on instead. The records in the `records/` folder beside a
specification's folder are checked with it.

Every specification is checked against the meta-model and against the
rules JSON Schema cannot express. It reports every problem in every
file, not only the first.

Every specification found is read before any is checked, so that a
reference into another specification (`<dependency>#/<pointer>`,
through a dependency with `specification` and `version`) resolves in
the one whose `info.name` the dependency names, when it is given in
the same run: its element is checked as a local one is, and the
dependency's version against that specification's `info.version`.
A reference whose specification is not given, or whose element is
blocked there by a must question, is not an error: it is counted as
unresolved, and `gaps` lists it (ADR-112).

An estate file, `specarch-estate.yaml`, found under a folder or
named, lists the modules' specifications by their `info.name` with
the folder each is in and the version the estate holds; it brings
each module's specification into the run, read once however often
it is named, so every reference between them resolves. Each module
is checked against its entry, as `module` at the module: its folder
holds a specification, whose `info.name` is the key and whose
`info.version` is the version listed, and its operations' and jobs'
`calls` do not come back to it through the other modules' (ADR-113).

```
specarch validate <paths>...
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

| Argument | What to give | Required |
|---|---|---|
| `<paths>` | Folders and files. A folder is searched for specifications, for implementation files outside one, and for estate files. One or more. | yes |

It reads:

- `{paths}`: Root files, the files under their stage folders, and implementation files.
- `records/ beside each specification's folder`: The change, defect, release, incident, commissioning and approval records of that specification.
- `` the specification named in each standalone implementation file's `implements` ``: Read to resolve that file's references.
- `each estate's modules, at their location`: The specification of every module an estate lists, read with the estate.

It writes no file.

On standard output: One line per diagnostic, `file:line:column: severity: /yaml/path: rule: message [id]`, sorted by file, then line, column, path, rule, message and id.

On standard error: A usage message on a usage error, the reason on an unreadable path, and a one-line count at the end, with the number of open questions and of unresolved references when there are any.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | every input is valid |   |
| 1 | at least one input has an error | Settle each error it prints at the file, line and path given, then run it again. |
| 2 | usage error, a path could not be read, or a folder holds no specification, no implementation file and no estate | Read the usage message or the reason on standard error, correct the command line or the path it names, and run it again. |

### specarch version

Print the program version and the meta-model versions it reads.

**Insight:** One version answers which SpecArch made a file; every generated file's header names it.

```
specarch version
```

Anyone who has the program runs it.

It writes no file.

On standard output: The program version, then one line for specifications and one for implementation files. Each line names the meta-model version a file is written in and, when there are any, the earlier versions still read until 1.0, each with a warning that the file is on an earlier version: `specifications: meta-model 0.3, and 0.2 and 0.1 until 1.0, with a warning`. The versions come from the schema the build embeds, the `specarch` enum of the specification schema and the `specarchImplementation` value of the implementation schema, the last being the current one, so the line cannot name a version the validator does not read.

| Exit status | It means | What to do |
|---|---|---|
| 0 | printed |   |
